title: What does the Aged Care Act 2024 require of aged care workers and providers for screening and training?
description: Who is an aged care worker, the Code of Conduct, police certificate or NDIS clearance rules, training conditions and penalties under the Aged Care Act 2024.
shortAnswer: The Aged Care Act 2024, in force since November 1, 2025, makes every registered provider screen its aged care workers and responsible persons, ensure workers have appropriate qualifications, skills or experience, and give them opportunities to develop capability. Workers, including volunteers and contractors, must personally comply with the Aged Care Code of Conduct, with civil penalties of up to 250 penalty units. Screening currently relies on a police certificate under three years old or an NDIS clearance.
keyTakeaways: An aged care worker under section 11(4) of the Act includes employees, independent contractors and volunteers of a registered provider and of its associated providers.
Section 152 makes worker screening, qualifications and training, and capability development conditions of registration for every kind of registered provider.
Under the Aged Care Rules 2025, most workers need a police certificate not more than 3 years old, an NDIS clearance, or a pending application with supervision and a statutory declaration.
Workers and responsible persons can each be liable for a civil penalty of 250 penalty units for breaching the Code of Conduct (sections 173 and 174), and can be banned.
Section 180 requires executives and other responsible persons to exercise due diligence, which includes keeping their own knowledge of the Act current.
regulator: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission, under the Aged Care Act 2024 administered by the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing
appliesTo: Registered providers in all seven provider registration categories, including the subscription trial
Aged care workers: employees, independent contractors and volunteers of a registered provider or its associated providers
Responsible persons: governing body members, executives, nursing managers and home or branch managers
Subcontracted and associated providers delivering funded aged care services on a registered provider's behalf

sections.heading: What did the Aged Care Act 2024 change for workers?

blocks.text: The Act moved aged care regulation from approved providers and their staff to registered providers, aged care workers and responsible persons, each with obligations that can be enforced against them directly. The commencement table of the [Aged Care Act 2024](https://www.legislation.gov.au/C2024A00104/latest/text) records that the whole Act commenced on November 1, 2025, fixed by Proclamation (F2025N00516), and the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing [confirms the new Act started on that date](https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/aged-care-act).

For workforce teams the practical changes are three. First, the definition of a worker now expressly reaches volunteers, contractors and staff of subcontractors. Second, screening and training are conditions of registration set out in the Act and detailed in the [Aged Care Rules 2025](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01173/latest/text), so a failure is a breach of registration. Third, the Aged Care Code of Conduct binds individuals, so a worker who breaches it is personally exposed.

This page covers the Act, the Code and the screening rules. The workforce training outcome in the strengthened Quality Standards (Outcome 2.9) and the annual incident, complaints and whistleblower training conditions are explained separately on the [Aged Care Quality Standards training](/regulations/aged-care-quality-standards-training) page.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the Act (compilation in effect from July 1, 2026) and the Aged Care Rules 2025 (compilation in effect from October 1, 2026) as at November 2026. The Rules are amended often; check the Federal Register of Legislation before relying on a section number.

sections.heading: Who counts as an aged care worker or a responsible person?

blocks.text: An aged care worker is any individual employed or otherwise engaged, including as a volunteer, by a registered provider to deliver funded aged care services, plus individuals working for an associated provider under its arrangement with the registered provider. A note to section 11(4) states that an individual engaged by a registered provider includes an independent contractor, and an individual who is a registered provider is also a worker.

A responsible person, under section 12, includes anyone responsible for the provider's executive decisions (expressly including governing body members), anyone with authority or significant influence over planning, directing or controlling its activities, a registered nurse with overall responsibility for nursing services, and anyone responsible for the day to day operations of a residential care home or service delivery branch. A responsible person is not also an aged care worker unless they are engaged to deliver services.

Section 11(6) makes the registered provider answerable for conduct of its associated providers as if it had engaged in that conduct. A home care provider that subcontracts cleaning or allied health therefore needs screening and Code of Conduct evidence for the subcontractor's people, not only its own payroll.

sections.heading: Which providers do the worker requirements apply to?

blocks.text: The worker screening and qualification conditions apply to every registered provider. Section 152-5 of the Rules prescribes "every kind of registered provider" for the section 152 condition, so it is not limited to residential care.

Registration is by category. Section 11(3) of the Act creates the residential care category, and section 11-5 of the Rules adds six more: home and community services; assistive technology and home modifications; advisory and support services; personal and care support in the home or community; nursing and transition care; and the subscription trial. The category matters for audits and for which Quality Standards apply, but not for whether a provider must screen its workers. The screening criteria do differ for workers delivering services only under the Commonwealth Home Support Programme (CHSP) or the National Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Flexible Aged Care Program (NATSIFACP), as the next section explains.

Before a person works, the provider must be able to show one of four clearance pathways in sections 152-20 and 152-21 of the Rules. Responsible persons have parallel requirements under sections 152-15 and 152-16.

blocks.text: For workers who deliver services only under CHSP or NATSIFACP, section 152-25 uses a different test: the certificate must not record a conviction for an offense involving a death, or, in the 5 years before the certificate, a conviction and imprisonment of at least one year for a sex related offense or an offense involving dishonesty.

Screening is not one and done. Providers must take reasonable measures to require workers to notify them of an NDIS exclusion decision, a suspended NDIS clearance, or a relevant conviction, and must not allow a worker to continue if satisfied on reasonable grounds that a disqualifying conviction has occurred. Because police certificates expire after 3 years for this purpose, a renewal register is part of the obligation.

blocks.title: National aged care worker screening
blocks.text: The Act defines an aged care worker screening check and an aged care worker screening database (section 379), linked to state and territory laws prescribed by the rules. As at November 2026, the Rules compilation in effect from October 1, 2026 does not prescribe any such state or territory law, so the police certificate and NDIS clearance pathways above remain the operative requirements.

sections.heading: What training and qualifications must providers ensure?

blocks.text: Section 152(1) of the Act requires providers to ensure workers meet any qualifications and training requirements in the Rules and are given opportunities to develop their capability. Section 152-35 of the Rules sets the baseline: aged care workers "must have appropriate qualifications, skills or experience to provide the funded aged care services that the provider delivers to individuals."

The Rules do not list courses or hours at this level. Instead they make the provider document how it met the test. Section 154-905 requires a record for each worker that includes how the provider ensured the worker has appropriate qualifications, skills or experience, and how the worker is given opportunities to develop capability. The same record holds the police certificate, statutory declaration or NDIS clearance, and, for documents received after commencement, the name of the person who checked it and the date. Section 154-910 requires those records to be kept for 7 years from the later of creation or last update.

In residential care, the Act also requires at least one registered nurse on site and on duty at all times at each approved residential care home (section 175), subject to time limited exemptions. Rostering and credential checks for registered nurses therefore sit alongside the worker record.

sections.heading: What does the Code of Conduct require of individual workers?

blocks.text: Every aged care worker and responsible person must comply with the Aged Care Code of Conduct, and the provider must take reasonable steps to ensure they do. Section 145 makes compliance, and reasonable steps to secure workers' compliance, a condition of registration. Sections 173 and 174 make non-compliance by a worker or responsible person a civil penalty provision carrying 250 penalty units.

The Code is set out in section 14-5 of the Rules as eight first person commitments. Among them, workers must "deliver funded aged care services in a safe and competent manner, with care and skill", act with integrity, honesty and transparency, promptly raise and act on concerns about quality and safety, and take all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to violence, discrimination, exploitation, neglect, abuse and sexual misconduct. A note to section 14-10 points to banning orders under section 498 of the Act as a further consequence. The Commission publishes [Code of Conduct guidance for workers](https://www.agedcarequality.gov.au/workers/aged-care-code-conduct/aged-care-code-conduct) that is suitable source material for induction.

Because the "reasonable steps" test in section 145 falls on the provider, evidence that each worker was taught the Code, understood it and knows how to raise a concern is the provider's main defense. A signed acknowledgment alone is weak evidence; a short scenario assessment is stronger, as explained in [policy attestation](/glossary/policy-attestation).

sections.heading: What duties and penalties apply to providers and executives?

blocks.text: Registered providers carry a statutory duty, and their executives carry a due diligence duty that includes keeping their own knowledge current. Section 179 requires a provider to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, that its conduct does not cause adverse effects to the health and safety of individuals receiving funded services. A serious failure attracts up to 1,000 penalty units for a body corporate, rising to 4,800 penalty units where it results in death, serious injury or illness.

Section 180 requires responsible persons under section 12(1)(a) or (b) to exercise due diligence. Due diligence includes reasonable steps "to acquire and maintain knowledge of requirements applying to registered providers" under the Act, to understand the services and their risks, and to ensure the provider has and uses appropriate resources and processes. Penalties are up to 150 penalty units for a serious failure and 500 penalty units where death, serious injury or illness results. That first limb is, in effect, a training obligation for board members and executives.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats the Act, the Rules and the Code as separate but connected obligation sets, and ties each worker role to the screening item, Code commitment and capability evidence it needs. When the Rules are amended, the framework shows which worker records and assessments depend on the changed section. More detail is on the [healthcare and life sciences](/industries/healthcare-life-sciences) page.

faqs.q: Do volunteers in aged care need a police certificate?
faqs.a: Yes, if they deliver funded aged care services. Section 11(4) of the Act includes volunteers in the definition of an aged care worker, and the Rules require each aged care worker to have a qualifying police certificate, an NDIS clearance, or an approved pending check arrangement.

faqs.q: Can an NDIS worker screening clearance be used instead of a police certificate?
faqs.a: Yes. The Aged Care Rules 2025 accept an NDIS clearance decision in force as one of the clearance pathways for aged care workers and responsible persons. The provider must still record the clearance and require the worker to report if it is suspended or an exclusion decision is made.

faqs.q: Can a new worker start before their police check comes back?
faqs.a: Yes, under conditions. The person must have a pending police certificate or NDIS screening application, be appropriately supervised, and give the provider a statutory declaration that they have no disqualifying convictions. The provider should record the declaration and track the check to completion.

faqs.q: Does the Act set mandatory training hours for aged care workers?
faqs.a: No. The Act and Rules require appropriate qualifications, skills or experience and opportunities to develop capability, and require the provider to record how it met that test. Specific training topics come from the Quality Standards and other conditions of registration, not from fixed hours.

faqs.q: How long must aged care worker screening records be kept?
faqs.a: Section 154-910 of the Rules requires worker records under section 154-905, including screening documents, to be kept for 7 years starting on the later of the day the record is first made or the day it was last updated.
